practices.name: Listen for F-sharp and E-flat pitch qualities on your own instrument
practices.skill: Explore intrinsic pitch qualities rather than merely higher/lower relationships or instrumental timbre.
source_instructions: Go to your own live instrument and listen to concert F-sharp and E-flat; the speaker describes F-sharp as vibrant/twangy and E-flat as softer/mellow.
Use these adjectives as hints, not visual-color associations or a demand for a concrete sensation.
Transposing instrumentalists use the written notes producing those concert pitches; a B-flat trumpet uses written G-sharp and F.
practices.presentation: Self-play and listen; the recorded examples illustrate the comparison but are not a required recognition test.
practices.response: Attend to each tone's subtle quality; no named or sung answer is required.

completion.details: Have a listen, then continue the master class. The closing reminder suggests a break and continuing fresh tomorrow; no count or accuracy threshold.

evidence.quote: quantification drills. Now for solo guitarists, what I'd like you to do is capo your guitar
up to F, like this, so that your E string now plays F. I'm playing here on synthesizer
now plays an F. First, figure out what your tones are now for each of your strings.
Now that you've got the capo on, then repeat the same drills you were doing with your open guitar strings.
Just play a string at random and see if you know which one it is.
But this time, call it the new pitch.
Your E string is now going to be your F string, so you have to call it F.
So go ahead and redo your guitar strings by ear with this new set of pitches.
First, we'll do single strings, then two strings at once, just the same way we did it before.
and you can even get someone else to help you at the end to test you
to make sure you really know those strings.
You don't have to pass any particular verification round.
Just work with the strings until you feel you know them.
